Mosca's inequality (x + y > z): x = 10, y = 5, z = 8 → migration would finish too late under this scenario. z is a planning assumption chosen per risk profile, not a prediction. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer is not publicly known to exist today.

Post-quantum maturity: Level 2 of 4 — post-quantum in use outside the critical paths. Next step: Extend post-quantum protection to the critical roles that stay classical, starting with what can be recorded today (wrapped keys, channel key exchange).

Methodology

The audit was performed by the QSI engine 1.3.0. Each analyzer emits facts (rule, parameters, evidence); finding texts are generated from the rule catalog. Methodology sources are listed under "Sources and normative documents".

Prioritization uses an explainable weighted model (severity, exploitability, exposure, confidentiality/integrity/availability impact weighted by the "Crypto exchange, custodian or wallet" profile, asset criticality, urgency, ease of remediation) with a confidence multiplier. CVSS v3.1 is applied only to technical vulnerabilities with a defined vector. Long-term quantum risks use Mosca's inequality; their severity is capped at Medium and they are never presented as exploitable vulnerabilities.

Finding classes: confirmed technical vulnerability; known vulnerable component (a dependency version named in an advisory; whether the affected code is reachable is assessed separately, and a component confirmed by review becomes a vulnerability); confirmed configuration error; potential cryptographic risk; long-term post-quantum risk; improvement recommendation; insufficient data. Heuristic findings are marked preliminary; analyst decisions are shown next to the findings.

Architecture overview

Static review of the source tree arc-node at 6e764023ee6515fe70573e123ed2db912a7207b4. 1135 files analysed; of 3265 files, 1461 are test, fuzzing, benchmark or example code and were left out, 669 are not read by any analyzer, 0 exceed the per-file limit and 0 did not fit the total limit. Files no analyzer reads include: .cargo/audit.toml, .config/nextest.toml, .dockerignore, .foundry-version, .github/CODEOWNERS. 685 files in build-output or dependency-cache directories (.git, .hg, .venv, __pycache__, build, dist, node_modules, target, vendor, venv) were not read. 750 files come from directories a .gitmodules pins and are read as shipped source rather than skipped as a dependency cache: contracts/lib/openzeppelin-contracts-upgradeable (459), contracts/lib/openzeppelin-contracts (291). No requests were sent to the owner's systems.

Recommendation

Triage the advisory; upgrade to a fixed version (1.51.6, 1.53.3) if it applies.

Improvement recommendationConfidence: Mediumpreliminary — requires further verification

The manifests mark them as such (devDependencies, "dev": true in package-lock.json, pnpm importers sections, [dev-dependencies]/[build-dependencies] reached through Cargo.lock, or — for yarn.lock, which records no scope at all — package.json reached through the lock graph), so they are not part of what ships.

Affected asset
dependencies:crates.io:non-runtime
Data source
OSV.dev
Detection method
OSV.dev querybatch lookup of exact versions; scope from devDependencies, package-lock.json dev flags, pnpm importers sections, the Cargo.lock graph rooted at the Cargo.toml tables, and — for yarn.lock, which records no scope — the lock graph walked from package.json. Where a runtime requirement cannot be resolved in a lock, that lock is left unclassified rather than risking a package being set aside wrongly.

Post-quantum assessment

Planning assumptions: x for key establishment, x for signatures, y are the defaults of the risk profile “Crypto exchange, custodian or wallet”, not the client's figures; with the client's actual lifetimes the verdict can change.

Post-quantum maturity: Level 2 of 4 — post-quantum in use outside the critical paths

  • In use: SLH-DSA — crates/pq-precompile/src/lib.rs
  • In use: SLH-DSA — crates/precompiles/src/bin/generate_pq_test_vectors.rs
  • In use: SLH-DSA — crates/precompiles/src/pq_test_vectors.rs
  • A post-quantum library is declared as a dependency

Next step: Extend post-quantum protection to the critical roles that stay classical, starting with what can be recorded today (wrapped keys, channel key exchange).

Levels: 0 none; 1 present, not wired; 2 in use outside the critical paths; 3 hybrid in a critical path; 4 post-quantum by default in the critical paths (root of trust, key wrapping, channel key exchange). Judged from code and manifests.

What the quantum-vulnerable algorithms do

RoleAlgorithms (files)IDFirst step
transaction and message signingECDSA (4), Ed25519 (1)QSI-2026-19421, QSI-2026-19422Follow each chain's post-quantum roadmap, avoid public-key reuse, and keep signers ready to add post-quantum signature schemes as chains adopt them
role not determinedEd25519 (4), ECDSA (2)QSI-2026-19420, QSI-2026-19423Classify each usage, record data lifetimes, and plan migration to ML-DSA (FIPS 204) or SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), in a hybrid/composite form where the ecosystem supports it; introduce an abstraction layer for crypto-agility

Roles are judged from file paths, function names and the code around each match; review confirms them. Root-of-trust keys and wrapped keys come first: they are hard to replace or can be recorded today.

z is a planning assumption chosen per risk profile, not a prediction. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer is not publicly known to exist today.

Quantum algorithms relevant to this inventory

Quantum algorithmEffectInventoried algorithms (rows)What it means for this audit
Shor's algorithm — elliptic-curve discrete logarithms
Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim		breaks ECDSA (9), Ed25519 (5)Elliptic-curve keys are expected to fall before RSA keys of comparable classical strength. On blockchains, coins whose public key is already on chain (reused addresses, pay-to-public-key and Taproot outputs) are exposed first; plan the move to post-quantum signatures and avoid key reuse in the meantime.
Grover's algorithm — key search and preimages
Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim		weakens (larger keys restore the margin) Keccak-256 (90), SLH-DSA (4)Not a break. 256-bit keys (AES-256, ChaCha20) keep a comfortable margin; AES-128 meets NIST category 1, while some authorities ask for 256-bit keys in quantum-resistant contexts (see the AES-128 entry). Prefer 256-bit keys for long-lived data; 256-bit hashes need no change for preimage resistance.
Brassard–Høyer–Tapp — collision search
Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim		weakens (larger keys restore the margin) Keccak-256 (90)256-bit hashes (SHA-256, SHA3-256) remain adequate for collision resistance; 160-bit hashes are already weak classically (SHA-1 collisions are practical). Use 384/512-bit hashes where NIST categories 4–5 are required.

Effects: breaks — replace the algorithm; weakens — larger keys or outputs restore the margin; included in standard parameters — no action at standard parameter sets; only with superposition queries — not applicable to ordinary deployments.

  • z is a planning assumption chosen per risk profile, not a prediction. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer is not publicly known to exist today.

QSI-2026-19466 · P2 · 60 daysroot-cause fix

Use OpenZeppelin ECDSA.recover with EIP-712 domain separation and nonces.

Rationale
Without s-value/zero-address checks and nonces, signatures may be malleable or replayable. ecrecover relies on secp256k1 ECDSA (quantum-vulnerable long-term).
Expected outcome
Re-run static analysis and add a unit/fuzz test that exercises the pattern.
Complexity
medium
Tests before change
Open line 148 in the supplied file contracts/lib/openzeppelin-contracts-upgradeable/lib/openzeppelin-contracts/contracts/utils/cryptography/ECDSA.sol and inspect the quoted lines (see evidence).
Tests after change
Re-run static analysis and add a unit/fuzz test that exercises the pattern.
Closure criteria
Re-run static analysis and add a unit/fuzz test that exercises the pattern.

QSI-2026-19421 · P4 · 90 daysroot-cause fix

Plan migration of Ed25519 to ML-DSA (FIPS 204) or SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), in a hybrid/composite form where the ecosystem supports it (or a hybrid scheme) once supported by your libraries, protocols and counterparties.

Rationale
Removes dependence on a quantum-vulnerable public-key primitive.
Expected outcome
The asset uses a NIST-standardized post-quantum or hybrid algorithm.
Complexity
high
Dependencies
Library/protocol support (e.g. OpenSSL ≥ 3.5, HSM firmware), interoperability with peers.
Side effects
Larger keys/signatures, possible performance and compatibility impact.
Tests before change
Interoperability tests in a staging environment.
Tests after change
Verify the negotiated/used algorithm on the production asset.
Closure criteria
Re-audit shows ML-DSA (FIPS 204) or SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), in a hybrid/composite form where the ecosystem supports it or a hybrid scheme in use.

  1. A. Chailloux, M. Naya-Plasencia, A. Schrottenloher — An Efficient Quantum Collision Search Algorithm and Implications on Symmetric Cryptography (ASIACRYPT 2017; IACR ePrint 2017/847) — IACR ePrint. https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/847 (peer-reviewed article: Õ(2^{2n/5}) time, O(n) qubits, Õ(2^{n/5}) classical memory)
  2. C. Chevignard, P.-A. Fouque, A. Schrottenloher — Reducing the Number of Qubits in Quantum Discrete Logarithms on Elliptic Curves (IACR ePrint 2026/280) — IACR ePrint. https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/280 (revision of a EUROCRYPT 2026 paper: 3.12n + o(n) qubits; for n = 256, 1193 qubits and 22 runs of 2^38.98 Toffoli gates)
  3. C. Zalka — Grover's quantum searching algorithm is optimal (Phys. Rev. A 60, 2746, 1999; arXiv:quant-ph/9711070) — APS. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.60.2746 (peer-reviewed article: optimal for any success probability; parallel search gains no more than splitting the space)
  4. Common Vulnerability Scoring System v3.1: Specification Document — FIRST. https://www.first.org/cvss/v3.1/specification-document (final)
  5. D. J. Bernstein — Cost analysis of hash collisions: Will quantum computers make SHARCS obsolete? (2009) — cr.yp.to. https://cr.yp.to/hash/collisioncost-20090823.pdf (paper dated 2009-08-23)
  6. D. Litinski — How to compute a 256-bit elliptic curve private key with only 50 million Toffoli gates (arXiv:2306.08585) — arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08585 (preprint (2023-06-14): 6000 modules × 1152 physical qubits, one key per 10 minutes under its architecture assumptions)
  7. FIPS 203 — Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard (ML-KEM) — NIST. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/203/final (final (August 2024))
  8. FIPS 204 — Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA) — NIST. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final (final (August 2024))

  11. J. Proos, C. Zalka — Shor's discrete logarithm quantum algorithm for elliptic curves (Quantum Inf. Comput. 3(4), 2003; arXiv:quant-ph/0301141) — Quantum Information & Computation. https://doi.org/10.26421/QIC3.4-3 (peer-reviewed article)
  12. L. K. Grover — A fast quantum mechanical algorithm for database search (STOC 1996) — ACM. https://doi.org/10.1145/237814.237866 (peer-reviewed article)
  13. M. Amy et al. — Estimating the cost of generic quantum pre-image attacks on SHA-2 and SHA-3 (SAC 2016; arXiv:1603.09383) — Springer / arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09383 (peer-reviewed article: SHA-256 about 2^153.8 surface-code cycles on 2^12.6 logical qubits; SHA3-256 about 2^146.5 cycles on 2^20)
  14. M. Cain et al. — Shor's algorithm is possible with as few as 10,000 reconfigurable atomic qubits (arXiv:2603.28627) — arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28627 (preprint (2026-03-30): P-256 in a few days with 26,000 physical neutral-atom qubits; RSA-2048 one to two orders of magnitude longer)
  15. M. Mosca — Cybersecurity in an Era with Quantum Computers: Will We Be Ready? (IEEE Security & Privacy, 2018) — IEEE. https://doi.org/10.1109/MSP.2018.3761723 (peer-reviewed article; source of the x + y > z migration inequality)
  16. M. Roetteler, M. Naehrig, K. Svore, K. Lauter — Quantum resource estimates for computing elliptic curve discrete logarithms (ASIACRYPT 2017) — IACR / arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06752 (peer-reviewed article: at most 9n + 2⌈log2 n⌉ + 10 qubits and 448 n^3 log2 n + 4090 n^3 Toffoli gates)
  17. NIST IR 8547 — Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards — NIST. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/ir/8547/final (final (2026-10-27; the initial public draft of November 2024 is obsoleted). Tables 2 and 4: ECDSA, EdDSA and RSA signatures, finite-field and elliptic-curve DH and MQV, and RSA key establishment are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035 at every key size — the draft deprecated only the 112-bit level. A composite (hybrid) key establishment stays FIPS 140-validatable while one input comes from an approved scheme. Repeats the federal deadlines of OMB M-26-15: post-quantum key establishment by 2030-12-31 and signatures by 2031-12-31 for high value assets and high impact systems)
